tip: 'Quatre à quatre' literally means 'four by four' – the image is taking the stairs four steps at a time, i.e. bounding down them fast.
'Il pouvait courir' = he was able to, a standing ability. Switch to 'il a pu' and it usually means he managed to, that one time.
Reflexive verbs use a pronoun: 'me', 'te', 'se', 'nous', 'vous', 'se'. 'Je me lève' = I get myself up.
Feelings usually live in the imparfait: 'avais faim' (were hungry) is the ongoing state, 'es rentré' (came home) the completed action framing it.
Age in the past is normally imparfait: 'tu avais dix ans' = you were ten. The move, 'as déménagé', is the one-off event.
No '-e' on 'coupé' here: in 'elle s'est coupé le doigt' the finger is the real object, so 'coupé' doesn't agree with 'elle'.
'Se faire mal' literally means 'make yourself hurt' – French builds hurting from 'faire' (to make), not from a verb 'to hurt'. 'Tu t'es fait mal ?' = did you make yourself hurt?
'Se tromper de' + noun = to get the wrong one: 'je me suis trompé de route' = I took the wrong road.
To apologize is to excuse yourself in French: 's'excuser'. 'Elle s'est excusée' = she excused herself. There's no separate verb for 'apologize'.
Feeling takes a reflexive here: 'se sentir'. 'Tu te sens bien' adds a 'te' ('yourself') that English drops – you don't just feel, you feel yourself.
This 'se' means 'each other', not 'themselves': 'elles se téléphonent' = they phone each other. The same little word covers both meanings – context decides which.
The imparfait is the backdrop, the passé composé the event: 'il pleuvait' (was raining) when 'nous sommes sortis' (we went out).
'En' plus the '-ant' form means 'while doing': 'en faisant du ski' = while skiing. It's French's compact way to pin one action to another going on at the same time.
French usually says the arm, not his arm, for body parts: 'il s'est cassé le bras'. The reflexive 'se' already tells you whose it is, so a possessive would be redundant.
'Pour' here means 'by', a deadline, not 'for': 'pour demain' = by tomorrow. French reuses the same 'pour' for purpose and for due-dates.
'Sans que' ('without') forces the subjunctive: 'sans que je le sache', not 'sais'. Some conjunctions flip the verb to subjunctive no matter how factual it feels.
Remembering is reflexive in French and drags 'de' along: 'tu te souviens de...' = do you remember...? Literally 'you remind yourself of'.
'Continuer' usually takes 'à' before the next verb: 'continuer à marcher' = keep walking. Lots of French verbs pin a following infinitive with 'à' or 'de', not directly.
'Il faut que' forces the subjunctive: it's 'prenne', not 'prend'. Necessity plus 'que' changes the verb's form.
'Quand' or 'lorsque' + passé composé marks the interrupting event. The other action is imparfait.
You're interested 'à' something in French, not 'in' it: 's'intéresser à'. 'Il s'intéresse à l'art' = interested in art. The verb picks 'à' and the English 'in' vanishes.
Complaining is reflexive and takes 'de': 'se plaindre de'. 'Il se plaint du temps' = complains about the weather ('du' = 'de' + 'le').
'Dormir' is to sleep, but 's'endormir' is to fall asleep. 'Il s'est endormi' = he dropped off – the reflexive marks the crossing into sleep, not the sleeping itself.
'Qui ait', not 'qui a': the hotel isn't real yet, you're still searching for one. Wanting something uncertain triggers the subjunctive.
After 'il faut que', 'être' turns into 'soit': 'que tout le monde soit prêt', never 'est'. One of the most irregular subjunctives.
'Finir par' = to end up doing something. The 'par' introduces the eventual outcome.
Own body parts usually take 'the', not 'her', in French: 's'est coupé les ongles' = cut her nails. The reflexive 'se' already tells you whose nails they are, so 'les' does the rest.
The object pronoun tucks inside the 'ne...pas' wrapper: 'je ne le sais pas'. The 'le' stays glued to the verb, not after 'pas'.
'S'entendre' literally means 'hear each other', but 'nous nous entendons très bien' = we get along great. In French, getting on well is a matter of hearing each other well.
'En' stands in for 'of it/some', and French won't drop it the way English does: 'tu en as assez' is literally 'do you have enough of it'.
